raw_response:
Based on the summarized question, I would evaluate SEPIA first for a broader self-hosted assistant and Kalliope for a voice-driven automation assistant. Rhasspy is also highly relevant as a DIY voice-control toolkit, with a substantial maintenance caveat. Leon is a candidate to investigate further rather than a verified recommendation.

I can offer a comparison grounded in project documentation, not firsthand ownership or listening-test experience. The summary expresses concern about Mycroft's longevity, but it does not make offline-only operation, a particular platform, a language, an update schedule or any specific feature mandatory.

### 1. SEPIA — the broadest documented assistant environment

SEPIA's official overview describes client apps backed by a server you host, with language understanding, chat and extendable services. That makes it a useful first evaluation if you want an assistant environment to customize. Its speech configuration matters: the client can use platform-provided speech engines or a separate offline recognition server. Select the latter if local speech processing is part of what you want; hosting the core alone does not settle that choice. [Project overview](https://sepia-framework.github.io/) · [Speech configuration](https://sepia-framework.github.io/tools/index.html). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn611704390view0","turn783437522view2"]}}

Assessment: mixed app/framework; whole assistant candidate; DIRECT_DOCUMENTED for the described self-hosted architecture. I have not verified recognition quality, installation on your hardware or continued maintenance.

### 2. Kalliope — useful when you want to define the actions yourself

Kalliope provides a framework that connects voice and other input signals to actions you compose. Its README documents Debian-family systems, including Raspberry Pi. This is a good fit for a configurable assistant whose main purpose is to carry out your chosen routines. [Official README](https://github.com/kalliope-project/kalliope/blob/master/README.md). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn783437522view0"}}

Check the speech-engine settings before evaluating privacy or independence: the documented default recognizer is Google, while CMUSphinx is listed as a self-hosted alternative. The synthesis options also include local engines such as Pico2wave. Those choices need to match your intended deployment. [Official settings](https://github.com/kalliope-project/kalliope/blob/master/docs/settings/settings.md). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn783437522view1"}}

Assessment: framework; whole candidate for a custom command/action assistant; DIRECT_DOCUMENTED for that role. These documents do not prove that it will understand your actual commands well or provide everything you expect from a general assistant.

### 3. Rhasspy — relevant for an offline voice layer, with a dated archival caveat

The versioned Rhasspy documentation describes offline voice processing, command templates and structured intents that can drive external automation. You supply the command definitions and connect their intents to actions in Home Assistant, Node-RED or another handler. Without that connection, recognition alone will not perform the task. [Versioned documentation](https://rhasspy.readthedocs.io/en/v2.4.20/). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn497339839view0"}}

The official repository now states that it was archived on October 6, 2025. Given your concern about longevity, I would treat it as a historical or DIY option requiring ownership of its maintenance, rather than assume it solves that concern. This is a later event: it could not have informed the July 2021 question. [Official repository](https://github.com/rhasspy/rhasspy). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn497339839view1"}}

Assessment: framework; partial contribution to the complete assistant behavior; CONDITIONAL_TRANSFER through the explicit intent-to-action integration. Archival is a caveat here, not a violation of an invented hard maintenance requirement.

### 4. Leon — keep on the investigation list

Leon's current official repository supports running a personal assistant on your own machine, but it describes unfinished 2.0 work and points to master for the previous version. My attempts to inspect the legacy README failed. I therefore cannot verify the precise voice setup of that version from the opened evidence. [Official repository](https://github.com/leon-ai/leon). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn799396163view0"}}

Assessment: app; intended whole candidate; INSUFFICIENT. The next useful check is whether the specific legacy release you would deploy documents a usable self-hosted voice path. A positive result would support a version-specific recommendation; an explicit lack of voice operation would rule out that release for this role.

### How I would evaluate longevity

I would first write down a few real commands you need, identify which parts of each setup are local and which call external services, then try the documented configuration with your own microphone and language. That is a proposed evaluation, not a test I performed. Source availability and an extensible architecture can make taking over maintenance more feasible, but neither guarantees that a project will continue.

There is an important date limitation: this question is dated July 22, 2021, while most evidence available here is undated live documentation. I have not established a complete 2021 snapshot. The Rhasspy archival notice and the later indexed Leon notice must not be treated as information available to the original questioner. No candidate's long-term survival or hands-on reliability has been verified.
